planting.note: Set divisions or plugs into moist, humus-rich soil along streambanks, woodland edges, or rain garden margins; seed benefits from a cold-moist stratification period before spring sowing.

directions: Grow this clump-forming avens in consistently moist soil at a woodland edge, streambank, or shaded rain garden where its large basal leaves and wiry flower stalks can spread gradually by rhizome. Small five-petaled yellow flowers open in late spring and early summer atop branching stems, drawing in mining bees, sweat bees, and hoverflies before giving way to bristly, hooked seed clusters that cling to fur and clothing for dispersal. It tolerates both partial shade and full sun as long as soil stays evenly moist, making it a useful transitional plant between a rain garden basin and drier surrounding beds. Cut back spent flower stalks after seed dispersal to keep the foliage clump tidy through summer.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in moist meadow or open-woodland soil; seed needs several weeks of cold-moist stratification before it will germinate reliably.

directions: This diminutive iris relative forms tufted, grass-like clumps that suit the front of a moist meadow planting, damp open woodland edge, or rock garden pocket. Star-shaped violet-blue flowers with bright yellow centers open on flattened stems for a few hours each morning through late spring and early summer, offering small native bees and syrphid flies an early-season pollen source. It self-sows modestly where soil stays moist and is not overly competitive, so it pairs well with other low, fine-textured native groundcovers. Because the flowering stems are so slender, mass it in drifts of a dozen or more plants for visual impact rather than planting singly.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Set plugs or divisions in consistently damp soil at a woodland edge or wet meadow margin; the elongated, spade-shaped leaves distinguish it from rounder-leaved native violets.

directions: Primrose-leaved violet spreads by slender stolons to knit together a low, semi-evergreen groundcover in soil that stays damp through the growing season, such as a ditch edge, seasonal wet meadow, or the moist fringe of a woodland path. White flowers marked with fine purple veining near the throat open in mid-spring above the elongated, oval leaves that give the plant its name. Like other native violets it serves as a larval host plant for great spangled and other fritillary butterflies, and its early pollen is valuable to small mining bees emerging in spring. Because it tolerates both partial shade and periodic standing water, it is a good choice for the damp transition zone around a rain garden.

planting.note: Plant divisions in wet, humus-rich soil in shaded seeps, streambanks, or bog garden margins where the mat-forming stolons can spread freely.

directions: This diminutive violet forms loose mats via creeping stolons in permanently damp, cool soil such as spring seeps, streambanks, and the shaded margins of bogs and fens. Tiny white flowers with faint purple veining at the throat appear in mid to late spring just above the small rounded leaves, providing early nectar and pollen for small native bees and serving as a larval host for fritillary butterflies. Because it spreads readily by stolons in consistently wet ground, it works well as a living mulch beneath taller moisture-loving shade perennials rather than as a stand-alone specimen. Avoid letting the soil dry out, since this species has little drought tolerance and will decline quickly in dry shade.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Set plugs into consistently moist to wet, neutral-to-alkaline soil in a fen-like rain garden pocket or partially shaded wet meadow; keep soil from drying out during establishment.

directions: Northern bog violet favors calcareous fens, wet prairies, and moist meadow edges, forming a low rosette of heart-shaped leaves topped by deep violet-purple flowers in mid-spring. It is one of the most important larval host plants for the regal fritillary and several other declining fritillary butterfly species, making it a high-value addition to a pollinator-focused wet meadow or rain garden planting. Give it steady moisture and full sun to partial shade; it does not tolerate prolonged drying between waterings. Plant it in small colonies rather than as isolated specimens, since fritillary caterpillars search out dense patches of host foliage in spring.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant divisions in consistently wet, acidic soil at a bog margin, wet meadow, or partly shaded streambank; established clumps spread slowly by rhizome.

directions: A cold-hardy northeastern aster of boggy meadows, wet thickets, and pond margins, rough-leaved aster is easily identified by its coarse, sandpaper-textured leaves and violet-blue, yellow-centered flower heads that open from late summer into fall. It thrives in consistently wet, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, making it a good match for the damp fringe of a rain garden or the edge of a shaded wetland planting. Its late bloom period supplies critical nectar for bumble bees and migrating monarchs when few other perennials are still flowering. Give it room to spread gradually by short rhizomes and avoid letting the site dry out, since it is intolerant of drought.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in saturated, acidic, sphagnum-rich soil in shaded bog or fen conditions; this species will not persist in ordinary garden soil that dries between waterings.

directions: This diminutive relative of the larger false Solomon's seal is a true peatland specialist, spreading by thin rhizomes through the wet, mossy floor of bogs, fens, and shaded coniferous swamps. In late spring it sends up a whorl of three narrow leaves topped by a short spike of small white star-shaped flowers, followed by red berries that provide food for small woodland birds. The flowers draw small native bees and flies during their brief bloom window. It is a specialty plant best suited to a constructed bog garden or shaded, permanently saturated container feature rather than a conventional perennial bed, since it needs constant moisture, high acidity, and cool root conditions to survive.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Set transplants in well-drained to average garden soil at a prairie edge, savanna, or lightly shaded woodland border; space generously since it spreads by rhizome into loose colonies.

directions: Yellow crownbeard is a rhizomatous prairie and savanna native that brightens open woodland edges and dappled-shade borders with clusters of bright yellow, ragged-rayed daisy flowers from early to midsummer. It grows readily in light shade beneath scattered trees as well as in full sun, tolerating average to dry soil once established and spreading gradually to form loose colonies rather than a tight clump. The flat-topped flower clusters attract a wide range of bees, including specialist long-horned bees, along with butterflies and beneficial wasps, and the winged leaf stalks give the plant a distinctive silhouette even before bloom. Divide congested clumps every few years to keep the colony vigorous and to share plants for a naturalized woodland-edge planting.
